newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-Maverick Leigh strikes blow for independent film makers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Maverick Leigh strikes blow for independent film makers.

text.p: Mike Leigh, maverick master of improvisation, delights in the blank page.
No script, no plot, just months of improvisation with a group of devoted actors.
That's the way this fiercely independent film director creates the quirky tales of British suburban life that have belatedly won him an international following.

He has never pandered to Hollywood but now finds himself feted by the mecca of world cinema with five Oscar nominations for "Secrets and Lies," a touching tale of the pain and mystery surrounding adoption.
He was particularly thrilled by the nomination for best original screenplay for a work that started life as "Untitled 95".

"I work up the screenplay with the actors. It involves much improvisation. This makes it all worthwhile," said Leigh. "Secrets and Lies" has already won London Critics, Cannes Film Festival and Golden Globe awards.

"We were not tailoring it for the American market but it speaks to people right across the board. People laughed and cried everywhere. The film crossed over and got to audiences who had not been able to see my stuff," he said.
Leigh spent nine months building up the story in collaboration with his actors. Brenda Blethyn, in line for a Best Actress award next Monday (March 24), revelled in his unorthodox style.
"We built the character from infancy, the geography of where she was born, her little idiosyncracies -- childhood injuries, how obedient she was, her sense of smell, the minutest detail,"
Leigh believes Blethyn could beat off tough opposition from Hollywood star Diane Keaton and fellow Britons Kristin Scott Thomas and Emily Watson to land the coveted Oscar.

"The sense I have is that the actors who vote for the Academy awards really do look at 'Secrets and Lies' and understand what Brenda is doing. It is a very extraordinary and very special piece of acting," he said.
REVELLING IN THE MUNDANE

Leigh revels in the mundane minutiae of daily life. Critic Clive James said imagine Mozart's opera "Cosi Fan Tutte" without the music and without the words plus cheap furniture and you have a Mike Leigh film.
Fellow writer Alan Bennett, another master of understated British gentility, hails Leigh's dialogue as "verbal muzak... hilarious in a play but deeply dreary in life".
Leigh, born in 1943, the son of a doctor and a nurse, spent his childhood immersed in the 14 cinemas in his north England neighbourhood.

His father mocked "the moonings of a stage-struck girlie" when he went to acting school at the prestigious Royal Academy of Dramatic Art. He was not a success, discovering belatedly that directing was his forte.
His first film, "Bleak Moments" in 1971, was financed by actor Albert Finney who came from Leigh's home town of Salford.
In 1977, he triumphed with "Abigail's Party" a stage play hastily recorded for television. The star was Alison Steadman, his wife for 20 years until they split up recently.
Leigh first tasted international success in 1993 when "Naked" won the Palme d'Or at the Cannes film festival.
Realism is his trademark. Rehearsals for a shouting match outside a London church were so realistic that a police car was called and detectives tried to break up the row.

Leigh accuses the Conservative government of failing to give the British film industry enough financial support. In a clash with members of parliament, he rejected charges that he was an elitist producing films for a minority.
"There is a minority of people in this country who do make arty, esoteric, non-populist films. But most of us are motivated by a commitment to entertainment, not lofty ideals," he said.
Now Leigh, once feted by arthouse fans, finds himself at the age of 53 under the most glamorous spotlight in showbusiness.
The self-confessed pessimist who looks on all the Hollywood hype with a quizzical gaze, is thrilled that his offbeat hit has struck a blow for independent film makers.
"I think what is important is that out there in the world we are making independent films. They're not getting interference from executives, idiots and boneheads and that's what is important."
